Indian Standard 


NON-AUTOMATIC WEIGHING INSTRUMENTS 
PART 1 TERMINOLOGY AND DEFINITIONS 


1 SCOPE 


This standard (Part 1) covers the terminology and their 
definitions used in this standard. 


2 GENERAL DEFINITIONS 


For the purpose of this standard, the following 
definitions shall apply. 


2.1 Weighing (Measuring) Instrument 


A weighing (measuring) instrument that serves to 
determine the mass of a body by using the action of 
gravity on this body. The instrument may also be used 
to determine other quantities, magnitudes, parameters 
or characteristics related to mass. 


2.2 Automatic and Non-automatic Weighing 
Instrument 


According to its method of operation, a weighing 
instrument is classified as an automatic or non- 
automatic weighing instrument. 


2.3 Non-automatic Weighing Instrument 


Instrument that requires the intervention of an operator 
during the weighing process, for example to deposit 
on or remove from the receptor, the load to be measured 
and also to obtain the result. The instrument permits 
direct observation of the weighing results either 
displayed or printed; both possibilities are covered by 
the word ‘indication’. 


NOTE — Terms such as ‘indicate’, ‘indicating component’ and 
their derivatives do not include printing. 


A non-automatic weighing instrument may be of the 
following type: 


a) Graduated or non-graduated type, and 
b) Self-indicating, semi-self-— indicating or non- 
self indicating type 


NOTE — In this standard, a non-automatic weighing instrument 
in called an ‘instrument’. 


2.3.1 Graduated Instrument 


Instrument allowing the direct reading of the complete 
or partial weighing result. 


2.3.2 Self-indicating Instrument 


Instrument in which the position of equilibrium is 
obtained without the intervention of an operator. 


2.3.3 Semi-self Indicating Instrument 


Instrument with a self-indication weighing range, in 
which the operator intervene to alter the limits of this 
range. 


2.3.4 Electronic Instrument 
Instrument equipped with electronic devices. 
2.3.5 Instrument with Price Scales 


Instrument that indicates the price to pay by means of 
price charts or scales related to a range of unit prices. 


2.3.6 Price-computing Instrument 


Instrument that calculates the price to pay based on the 
indicated mass and the unit price. 


2.3.7 Price-labelling Instrument 


Price computing instrument that prints the weight value, 
unit price and price to pay for prepackages. 


2.3.8 Self-service Instrument 


Instrument that intended to be operated by the customer. 


2.4 Indication Provided by an Instrument 
2.4.1 Primary Indication 


Indications, signals and symbols that are subject to 
requirements of this specification. 


2.4.2 Secondary Indications 

Indication, signals and symbols that are not primary 
indications. 

3 CONSTRUCTION OF AN INSTRUMENT 

In this standard the term ‘device’ is used for any means 
by which a specific function is performed, irrespective 
of the physical realization, such as by 
a mechanism or a key initiating an operation; the device 
may be a small part or a major portion of an instrument. 
3.1 Main Device 

3.1.1 Load Receptor 

Part of the instrument intended to receive the load. 
3.1.2 Load-Transmitting Device 


Part of the instrument for transmitting the force 
produced by the load acting on the load receptor, to 
the load-measuring device. 


3.1.3 Load-Measuring Device 


Part of the instrument for measuring the mass of the 


IS 16514 (Part 1) : 2018 


load by means of an equilibrium device for balancing 
the force coming from the load transmitting device, and 
an indicating or printing device. 

3.2 Module 


Part of an instrument, which performs a specific 
function, may be examined separately and is subject to 
specified partial error limits. 


3.3 Electronic Parts 


3.3.1 Electronic Device 


A device employing electronic sub-assembly and 
performing a specific function. An electronic device is 
usually manufactured as a separate unit and can be 
independently tested. 


NOTE — An electronic device, as defined above, may be a 
complete instrument (for example, instrument for direct sales 
to the public) or parts of an instrument (for example, printer, 
indicator). 


3.3.2 Electronic Sub-assembly 


A part of an electronic device, employing electronic 
components and having a recognizable function of its 
own (for example: A/D converter, display matrix) 


3.3.3 Electronic Component 

The smallest physical entity that uses electron or hole 
conduction in semi-conductors, gases or in a vacuum. 
3.4 Indication Device of a Weighing Instrument 


Part of the load-measuring device on which the direct 
reading of the result is obtained. 


3.4.1 Indicating Component 
Component indicating the equilibrium and/or the result. 


3.4.1.1 On an instrument with one position of 
equilibrium it indicate only the equilibrium (so-called 
zero). 


3.4.1.2 On an instrument with several positions of 
equilibrium it indicates both the equilibrium and the 
result. On an electronic instrument, this is the display. 


3.4.2 Scale Mark 


A line or other mark on an indicating components 
corresponding to specified value of mass. 


3.4.3 Scale Base 

An imaginary line through the centers of all the shortest 
scale marks. 

3.5 Auxiliary Indicating Devices 

3.5.1 Device for Interpolation of Reading (Vernier) 


Device connected to the indicating element and sub- 
dividing the scale of an instrument, without special 
adjustment. 


3.5.2 Complementary Indicating Device 


Adjustable device by means of which it is possible to 


estimate, in units of mass, the value corresponding to 
the distance between a scale mark and the indicating 
component. 


3.5.3 Indicating Device with a Differentiated Scale 
Division 

Digital indicating device of which the last figure after 
the decimal sign is clearly differentiated from other 
figures. 


3.6 Extended Indicating Device 


A device temporarily changing the actual scale interval 
(d) to a value less than the verification scale interval 
(e) following a manual command. 


3.7 Supplementary Devices 
3.7.1 Levelling Device 


Device for setting an instrument to its reference 
position. 


3.7.2 Zero-Setting Device 


Device for setting the indication to zero when there is 
no load on the load receptor. 


3.7.2.1 Non-automatic zero-setting device 
Device for setting the indication to zero by an operator 
3.7.2.2 Semi-automatic zero setting device 


Device for setting the indication to zero automatically 
following a manual control. 


3.7.2.3 Automatic zero-setting device 


Device for setting the indication to zero automatically 
without the intervention of an operator. 


3.7.2.4 Initial zero-setting device 


Device for setting the indication to zero automatically 
at the time the instrument is switched on and before it 
is ready for use. 


3.7.3 Zero-Tracking Device 


Device for maintaining the zero indication within 
certain limits automatically. 


3.7.4 Tare Device 


a) Device for setting the indication to zero when 
a load is on the load receptor; without altering 
the weighing range for net loads (additive tare 
device) or reducing the weighing range for net 
loads (subtractive tare device) 


b) It may function as. 


1) anon-automatic device (load balanced by 
an operator); 


2) a semi-automatic device (load balanced 


automatically following a single manual 
command); and 


3) an automatic device (load balanced 
automatically without the intervention of 
an operator). 


3.7.4.1 Tare-balancing device 


Tare device without indication of the tare value when 
the instrument is loaded. 


3.7.4.2 Tare-weighing device 


Tare device that stores the tare value and is capable of 
indication or printing it whether or not the instrument 
is loaded. 


3.7.5 Present Tare Device 


Device for subtracting a present tare value from a gross 
or net weight value and indicating the result of the 
calculation. The weighing range for net loads is reduced 
accordingly. 


3.7.6 Locking Device 


Device for immobilizing all or part of the mechanism 
of an instrument. 


3.7.7 Auxiliary Verification Device 


Device permitting separate verification of one or more 
main device of an instrument. 


3.7.8 Selection Device for Load Receptors and Load 
Measuring Devices 


Devices for attaching one or more load receptors to 
one or more load measuring devices, whatever 
intermediate load transmitting device are used. 


3.7.9 Indication Stabilizing Device 


Device for maintaining a stable indication under given 
conditions. 


4 METROLOGICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF 
AN INSTRUMENT 


4.1 Weighing Capacity 
4.1.1 Maximum Capacity (Max) 


Maximum weighing capacity, not taking into account 
the additive tare capacity. 


4.1.2 Minimum Capacity (Min) 


Value of the load below which the weighing results, 
may be subject to an excessive relative error. 


4.1.3 Self-Indication Capacity 


Weighing capacity within which equilibrium is obtained 
without the intervention of an operator. 


IS 16514 (Part 1) : 2018 


4.1.4 Weighing Range 
Range between the minimum and maximum capacities. 
4.1.5 Extension Interval of Self-indication 


Value by which it is possible to extend the range of 
self-indication within the weighing range. 


4.1.6 Maximum Tare Effect (T = + .... T=—....) 


Maximum capacity of the additive tare device or the 
subtractive tare device. 


4.1.7 Maximum Safe Load (Lim) 


Maximum static load that can be carried by the 
instrument without permanently altering its 
metrological qualities. 


4.2 Scale Divisions 


4.2.1 Scale Spacing (Instrument with Analog 
Indication) 


Distance between any two consecutive scale marks, 
measured along the scale base. 


4.2.2 Actual Scale Interval (d) 
Value expressed in units of mass of, 


a) the difference between the values 
corresponding to two consecutive scale marks, 
for along indication, or 


b) the difference between two consecutive 
indicated values, for digital indication. 


4.2.3 Verification Scale Interval (e) 


Value expressed in units of mass, used for the 
classification and verification of an instrument 


4.2.4 Scale Interval of Numbering 


Value of the difference between the two consecutive 
numbered scale marks. 


4.2.5 Number of Verification Scale Intervals (Single- 
Interval Instrument) 


Quotient of the maximum capacity and the verification 
scale interval: 


n= Max/e 
4.2.6 Multi-Interval Instrument 


Instrument having one weighing range, which is divided 
into partial weighing ranges each with different scale 
intervals, with the weighing range determined 
automatically according to the load applied, both on 
increasing and decreasing loads. 


4.2.7 Multiple Range Instrument 


Instrument having two or more weighing ranges with 


IS 16514 (Part 1) : 2018 


different maximum capacities and different scale 
intervals for the same load receptor, each range 
extending from zero to its maximum capacity. 


5 METROLOGICAL PROPERTIES OF AN 
INSTRUMENT 


5.1 Discrimination 


Ability of an instrument to react to small variation of 
load. The discrimination threshold, for a given load, is 
the value of the smallest additional loads that, when 
gently deposited on or removed from the load receptor 
causes a perceptible change in the indication. 


5.2 Repeatability 


Ability of an instrument to provide results that agree 
one with the other when the same load is deposited 
several times and in a practically indicate way on the 
load receptor under reasonably constant test 
conditions. 


5.3 Durability 


Ability of an instrument to maintain its performance 
characteristics over a period of use. 


5.4 Warm-up Time 


The time between the moment power is applied to an 
instrument and the moment at which the instrument is 
capable of complying with requirements. 


6 INDICATIONS AND ERRORS 
6.1 Methods of Indication 
6.1.1 Balancing by Weights 


Value of meteorological controlled weights that balance 
the load (taking into account the reduction ratio of the 
load) 


6.1.2 Analogue Indication 


Indication enabling the evaluation of the equilibrium 
position to a fraction of the scale interval. 


6.1.3 Digital Indication 


Indication in which the scale marks are composed of a 
sequence of a aligned figures that do not permit 
interpolation to fractions of the scale interval. 


6.2 Weighing Results 


NOTE — The following definitions apply only when the 
indication has been zero before the load has been applied to 
the instrument. 


6.2.1 Gross Value (G) 


Indication of the weight of a load on an instrument with 
no tare or preset tare device in operation. 


6.2.2 Net Value (N) 


The weight value of a load, determined by a tare- 
weighing device. 


6.2.3 Tare Value (T) 

The weight value of load, determined by a tare weighing 
device. 

6.3 Other Weight Values 

6.3.1 Preset Tare Value (PT) 


Numerical value, representing a weight that is 
introduced into the instrument. ‘Introduced’ includes 
such as keying in, recalling from data storage, or 
inserting through an interface. 


6.3.2 Calculated Net Value 


Value of the difference between a gross or net weight 
value and a preset tare value. 


6.3.3 Calculated Total Weight Value 

Calculated sum of more than one weight value and/or 
calculated net value. 

6.4 Reading 

6.4.1 Reading by Simple Juxtaposition 


Reading of the weighing result by simple juxtaposition 
of consecutive figures giving the weighing result, 
without the need of calculation. 


6.4.2 Overall Inaccuracy of Reading 


The overall inaccuracy of reading of an instrument with 
analog indication is equal to the standard deviation of 
the same indication, the reading of which is carried out 
under normal conditions of use by several observers. 
It is customary to make at least ten readings of the 
results. 


6.4.3 Rounding Errors of Digital Indication 


Difference between the indication and the result the 
instrument would give with analogue indication. 


6.4.4 Minimum Reading Distance 


The shortest distance that an observer is able to freely 
approach the indicating device to take a reading under 
normal conditions of use. The approach is considered 
to be free for observer, if there is a clear space of at 
least 0.8 m in front of the indicating device (see Fig. 1). 


6.5 Errors 
6.5.1 See Fig. 2 for illustration of certain terms used: 
6.5.2 Error (of Indication) 


The indication of an instrument minus the 
(conventional) true value of the mass. 


IS 16514 (Part 1) : 2018 


Indicating device 


The minimum reading distance is S; however, if S < 0.8 m, then the minimum distance is L. 
Fic. 1 INDICATION OF MINIMUM READING DISTANCE 


6.5.3 Intrinsic Error 
The error of an instrument under reference conditions. 
6.5.4 Initial Intrinsic Error 


The initial intrinsic error of an instrument is as 
determined prior to the performance and span stability 
tests. 


6.5.5 Maximum Permissible Error 


Maximum difference, positive or negative, allowed by 
regulation between the indication of an instrument and 
the corresponding true value, as determined by 
reference standard masses, with the instrument being 
at zero at no-load, in the reference position. 


6.5.6 Fault 


The difference between the error of indication and the 
intrinsic error of an instrument. 


NOTE — Principally, a fault is the result of an undesired change 
of data contained in or flowing through an electronic instrument. 


6.5.7 Significant Fault 
A fault greater than e. 


NOTE — For a multi-interval instrument, the value of e is that 
appropriate to the partial weighing range. 


The following are not considered to be significant 
faults, even when they exceed e: 


a) Faults arising from simultaneous and mutually 
independent causes in the instrument. 


b) Faults implying the impossibility to perform 
any measurement. 

c) Faults being so serious that they are bound to 
be noticed by all those interested in the result 
of measurement. 


d) Transitory faults being momentary variations 
in the indication which cannot be interpreted, 
memorized or transmitted as a measuring 
result. 


6.5.8 Durability Error 


The difference between the intrinsic error over a period 
of use and the initial intrinsic error of an instrument. 


6.5.9 Significant Durability Error 


6.5.9.1 A durability error greater than e 
NOTES 


1 A durability error can be due to mechanical wear and tear of 
due to drift and aging of electronic parts. The concept of 
significant durability error apples only to electronic parts. 


2 For a multi-interval instrument, the value of e is that 
appropriate to the partial weighing range. 


6.5.9.2 The following are not considered significant 
durability error, even when they exceed e: 


Errors occurring after a period of instrument use that 
are clearly the result ofa failure of a device/component, 
or of a disturbance and for which the indication: 


a) Cannot be interpreted, memorized, or 
transmitted as a measurement result/or; 


IS 16514 (Part 1) : 2018 


E

E = error of indication

b) Implies the impossibility to perform any 
measurement, or 

c) Is so obviously wrong that it is bound to be 
noticed by all those interested in the results 
of measurement. 


6.5.10 Span Stability 


The capability of an instrument to maintain the 
difference between the indication of weight at maximum 
capacity and the indication at zero ever a period of use 
within specified limits. 


7 INFLUENCE AND REFERENCE CONDITIONS 
7.1 Influence Quantity 


A quantity that is not the subject of the measurement 
but which influences the values of the measure and or 
the indication of the instrument. 


7.1.1 Influence Factor 


An influence quantity having a value within the 
specified rated operating conditions of the instrument. 


7.1.2 Disturbance 


An influence quantity having a value within the limits 
specified in this specification but outside the specified 
rated operating conditions of the instrument. 


7.2 Rated Operating Conditions 


Conditions of use, giving the range of values of 
influence quantities for which the metrological 
characteristics are intended to lie within the specified 
maximum permissible errors. 


IS 16514 (Part 1) : 2018 


7.3 Reference Conditions 


A set of specified values of influence, factors fixed to 
ensure valid inter-comparison of the results of 
measurements. 


7.4 Reference Positions 

Positions of the instrument at which its operation is 
adjusted. 

8 PERFORMANCE TEST 


A test to verify whether the equipment under test (EUT) 
is capable of performing its intended functions.

Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed

needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards
